title: Homeschool record keeping template you can keep using
dek: Record the date, what was actually covered and one useful observation. Add evidence when it matters, and keep legal requirements separate.
metaDescription: Copy a simple homeschool record keeping template with dates, lesson references, observations and evidence. Includes a free printable record sheet.

sources.name: Florida Legislature: home education programmes, section 1002.41
sources.note: Official statutory example of a contemporaneous activity log, reading-material titles and work samples. Not a national record-keeping standard.

paragraphs: A usable homeschool record keeping template records the date, the subject and lesson or activity, what actually happened, and a short observation or evidence reference when useful. Keep a separate place for required attendance, assessments and legal filings. A learning log can support your records, but it does not automatically satisfy every state's rules.

The record is easy to postpone when the lesson has already taken the morning. Then a few weeks pass and you remember that there was science, but not which experiment, what changed, or where the photo went. The template's job is to leave a small trail while the details are still available.

This guide is for US homeschool parents who want a practical daily record on paper, in a spreadsheet or in a chosen app. It is not a curriculum, a grading system or a legal compliance certificate. Check the requirements for your child's actual educational route before deciding what must be kept or submitted.

body.heading: Copy these four columns
rows: Write the actual date
Name the book, unit, lesson or activity
Record completed, partly completed or changed work
Note a useful observation or where a sample is kept
Keep dates consistent
Use a reference you can find again
Do not copy a plan as if it happened
Leave this short when nothing more is needed

body.heading: Make the first entry small and specific
items: Choose one place for each child's record. Add the child's name or identifier where more than one child uses the same sheet.
After the learning activity, record the actual date and enough detail to identify the work later.
Write what happened rather than what was scheduled. Mark unfinished or changed work without turning the entry into a judgment about the child.
Add an observation or sample reference if it helps explain progress or a question to revisit.
Check separately that required attendance, subject, assessment and filing records are being maintained under the rules that apply.

body.heading: A week of invented entries
body.intro: These examples show the level of detail, not a recommended grade-level timetable or evidence of a real child's progress.
rows: Monday: fractions, lesson 8
Compared halves and quarters with paper strips
Ask for an explanation without strips next time
Tuesday: reading, chapter 4
Read together; discussed why the character left
Book title on the reading list; no additional sample needed
Wednesday: planned writing session
Stopped after the opening sentence; discussed the idea aloud
Try a spoken outline before writing
Thursday: seed observation
Measured and sketched two seedlings
Sketch in science folder, dated Thursday

body.heading: An observation is more useful than a performance label
paragraphs: 'Difficult' tells you how the session felt, but may not explain what to do next. 'Could compare the strips but could not explain the relationship without them' names a specific question. You do not need that much detail for every activity. Save it for work where the next decision depends on what you noticed.

Likewise, 'completed' and 'understood' are not interchangeable. A child can finish a worksheet with help, explain an idea orally without producing a page, or need another approach. Use [checking whether learning stuck](/guides/how-to-check-if-your-child-learned-something) when you need a better follow-up than another tick.
Do not turn the log into continuous testing. Its purpose is to support teaching and preserve a record, not to force a score onto every conversation, book or outing.

body.heading: Keep legal requirements beside the template, not inside a guess
paragraphs: As one jurisdiction-specific example, [Florida's home-education statute](https://wwwo.leg.state.fl.us/Statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=1000-1099%2F1002%2FSections%2F1002.41.html%2F) describes an activity log made as instruction happens, reading-material titles and samples of the student's work. That example does not tell a parent in another state what their records must contain.

Find your current official rules and record the required items, deadlines and retention arrangements separately. Our [requirements verification guide](/guides/homeschool-record-keeping-requirements-by-state) explains that process. If an evaluator, school or authority requests records, confirm what is required rather than sending every private family note by default.

body.heading: Use the record for the next teaching decision

items.line: We completed this activity with help. Before moving on, I want to check whether the idea makes sense without the same prompt. I will note what happens, not assume the tick settled it.
Here is the dated log and the samples it refers to. Which additional records are required for this review, and where can I find that requirement in the current guidance?

body.heading: When the record falls behind
items: Restart with today's actual work. Do not leave a growing blank period because the earlier pages are incomplete.
Reconstruct older entries from dated work, reading lists and other evidence where possible, marking uncertain dates honestly.
Do not backfill a weekly plan as a completed attendance or learning record. Keep the difference visible.
Use [catching up on homeschool records](/guides/how-to-catch-up-on-homeschool-records) for a larger gap, and ask the relevant authority or adviser promptly if a required deadline is involved.

items.q: Do I need an entry for every minute of homeschooling?
items.a: Not as a universal rule. This template is a learning log, not a national attendance requirement. Keep any hours, days, subjects or other evidence required for your situation separately and accurately. The useful level of detail is enough to identify actual work and support the next teaching or record-keeping decision.

items.q: Can I use the same activity entry for two children?
items.a: You can record a shared activity once for logistics, but keep each child's involvement and evidence identifiable where needed. Children may do different work or understand different parts of the same topic. Do not automatically copy the same result to everyone just because they sat at the same table.

items.q: Should I scan every worksheet into the log?
items.a: Not automatically. Keep the material your applicable rules require and useful samples that explain the work. A dated reference to where a sample is stored may be more manageable than attaching everything. Check submission and retention requirements before discarding originals or assuming a digital copy is sufficient.

body.heading: A record you will open tomorrow
paragraphs: Use the smallest record that preserves the information you actually need. For selecting evidence across a year, read [what goes in a homeschool portfolio](/guides/what-goes-in-a-homeschool-portfolio). The log and portfolio serve related but different purposes.

If keeping separate subjects and records for several children is the difficult part, [Homeschooling Companion](/shop/homeschooling-companion) is an optional organiser, not a curriculum or a compliance guarantee. The free record sheet here works on its own.

visuals.title: The smallest useful entry

steps.label: When
steps.detail: The actual date, marked uncertain if reconstructed.

steps.label: What
steps.detail: Subject, activity and a lesson or material reference.

steps.label: What happened
steps.detail: Completed, changed or unfinished work, not just the plan.

steps.label: What to keep
steps.detail: A useful observation, evidence location or next question.

visuals.caption: A completed activity is not automatically proof of understanding.
visuals.alt: Four learning-log fields identify the date, specific work, what actually happened and the evidence or follow-up needed.

visuals.title: Use the record, then keep moving

steps.label: Record
steps.detail: Leave a dated trail after the activity.

steps.label: Review
steps.detail: Notice what needs evidence or another explanation.

steps.label: Adjust
steps.detail: Choose the next small teaching step and record its result.

visuals.caption: Keep statutory attendance and filing obligations as a separate check.
visuals.alt: A three-step record, review and adjust loop turns a short learning log into a practical next teaching decision.

worksheet.title: Homeschool learning record
worksheet.prompt: Record actual learning activity and the information worth carrying into the next session.
fields: What happened, including changes or unfinished work
Separate legal record or filing to check
